title: A History of the World in 6 Glasses
author: Tom Standage
target_audience: Readers curious about the relationship between culture and consumables
core_themes: The influence of beverages on human civilization
Interconnection between culture, economics, and everyday commodities
How daily life and history are entwined
primary_purpose: To illustrate the pivotal role that six key beverages—beer, wine, spirits, coffee, tea, and Coca-Cola—have played in shaping human society, culture, trade, and international relations throughout history.

structure_format.organization: Divided into six main sections, each focusing on one beverage and its historical significance; prologue and epilogue frame the narrative
features: Accessible narrative linking everyday items to major world events
Contextualization of global shifts through a food-and-drink lens
Additional notes and references at the end

key_concepts_lessons: Each beverage embodies the technological advancements, social structures, and values of the era in which it became popular.
Beer and wine contributed to the development of ancient civilizations through ritual, nutrition, and social cohesion.
Distilled spirits were central to exploration, colonization, and the slave trade.
Coffee and tea fueled intellectual revolutions and global commerce during the Enlightenment and Industrial Revolution.
Coca-Cola represents globalization, American influence, and modern consumer culture.
The history of what we drink mirrors larger patterns in economics, innovation, politics, and society.
notable_features: Clever use of everyday drinks to structure world history
Blends social, political, and economic history
Connects cultural developments to daily habits
Strong narrative thread linking disparate historical periods
cultural_historical_context: Published in the early 21st century amid growing interest in food history, global interconnectedness, and microhistory approaches. The book draws on themes of globalization and the idea that everyday items can reveal deep insights into world events.
reception_impact: Well-received for its originality and engaging storytelling
Frequently used as a supplemental text in high school and college history classes
Praised as a model of popular history writing
Inspired further works examining history through the lens of food, objects, or daily life
comparable_titles: Salt: A World History by Mark Kurlansky
Guns, Germs, and Steel by Jared Diamond
An Edible History of Humanity by Tom Standage
Cod: A Biography of the Fish that Changed the World by Mark Kurlansky
